summary: Penumbra is a web app that answers the two questions behind every lunar south-pole landing — will we have power? and can we talk to Earth? — for any site and date in seconds. It shows the Sun and the Earth above the real local horizon built from NASA LRO LOLA topography, with live GPU-rendered shadows over the polar map, one-year illumination maps that reveal peaks of near-eternal light, a 360° horizon panorama, a 3D "astronaut's eye" view, and a timeline with time-to-sunset and time-to-Earthset, a battery simulation and Deep Space Network coverage. Planners can slip the landing date by a day, compare scenarios side by side, scan a whole year of landing dates across sites in one heatmap, or re-run the whole mission over the landing ellipse to see what happens if the lander misses its target by a few hundred metres. Educators and the public get one-click lessons that make the strangeness of the pole visible. Everything runs in the browser; the Sun and Earth elevations it computes agree with NASA/JPL Horizons within 9 arcseconds, and its terrain-aware illumination reproduces published 20-year averages at the Connecting Ridge to within 0.3 percentage points.
details:
What it does. Pick a curated site (Connecting Ridge, Shackleton rim and floor, de Gerlache rim, Malapert Massif, Mons Mouton, Nobile Rim 2, IM-1/IM-2, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, Chang'e-4, Apollo 11/17) or click anywhere on the polar map. Choose a landing date and a mission window. Penumbra then shows:
• a horizon panorama with the LOLA terrain silhouette, the Sun and Earth tracks over the whole window, true angular sizes and Earth phase;
• a live shadow map of the south pole in which every pixel is ray-marched toward the Sun (or the Earth) on the GPU, so shadows sweep around the pole as you scrub time;
• a timeline of sunlight (visible fraction of the solar disk), Earth visibility and both together, plus Sun elevation vs. the terrain beneath it;
• now metrics: Sun/Earth elevation and azimuth, array output in W/m², time to sunset/sunrise and Earthset/Earthrise;
• mission KPIs: sunlight %, direct-to-Earth %, Sun+Earth %, longest darkness, longest comm gap, mean array power, battery needed to survive the longest darkness, flat vs. vertical panel;
• mission-window maps: sunlight % and Earth-in-view % over the whole window, averaged over 128 instants on the GPU, with the best-lit spot in view marked;
• 3D terrain and an astronaut's-eye view with the same ray-traced shadows, the true-size Sun and the Earth with its real phase; zoomed in on the Earth, the DSN antennas appear on its disk, green when in line of sight and red when hidden by the lunar terrain;
• power-system simulation (array, load, battery; rover / CLPS lander / habitat presets): does the battery survive the window?
• Deep Space Network coverage: a direct-to-Earth link needs Goldstone, Madrid or Canberra to see the Moon and to be in line of sight of the site itself. Seen from the south pole Canberra sits ~0.5° above Earth's centre and Goldstone/Madrid ~0.5° below, so modelling the antennas (not Earth's centre) changes the answer when Earth grazes the horizon: at Mons Mouton in 2027 the link drops from 98.1% to 91.8%;
• linked horizon and map: hover the skyline and the map traces the ridge that blocks the Sun at that azimuth, kilometres away;
• off-target touchdown: one click re-runs the mission at 19 points of a ±250 m to ±5 km landing ellipse. On Connecting Ridge in March 2027 a ±500 m ellipse spans 23–99% sunlight, and a CLPS-class battery survives at only 7 of the 19 touchdown points. Real landers do miss: IM-2 Athena came down about 250 m from its target in March 2025, inside a small crater, and its mission ended the next day.

Planners can press ±1 day to see a schedule slip, list the best landing dates of the next 12 months for the chosen site, + Compare to stack scenarios, and open the When & where heatmap (every site × every landing day of a year) to find viable alternatives when a date or location changes. A Verify in JPL Horizons button opens the identical query in NASA's Horizons API, a Share link reopens the exact scenario (including the comparison), CSV export hands the time series to other tools, and a printable one-page mission brief goes to a review board. A 45-second guided tour and eight one-click lessons serve educators and the public.

Try these scenarios (one click each). Earth from Connecting Ridge: https://valtielcs.github.io/penumbra/#site=c1&start=2027-01-08T00:00&days=7&t=2027-01-15T00:00&vm=eye&look=earth · a year of sunlight around Shackleton: https://valtielcs.github.io/penumbra/#site=c1&start=2027-01-01T00:00&days=365.25&layer=3&mv=-6,-4,70 · missing the target by 500 m: https://valtielcs.github.io/penumbra/#site=c1&start=2027-03-01T00:00&days=14&t=2027-03-08T12:00&ellipse=0.5 · when to land on Mons Mouton: https://valtielcs.github.io/penumbra/#site=mou&start=2027-03-01T00:00&days=14&best=1 · which DSN antenna keeps the link: https://valtielcs.github.io/penumbra/#site=mou&start=2027-03-01T00:00&days=29.53&t=2027-03-24T02:00&vm=eye&look=earth

How it works. The Sun and Moon positions (Astronomy Engine) are rotated into the Moon-fixed Mean-Earth frame with the IAU lunar rotation model, the same frame as LOLA and Horizons' MOON_ME. Topocentric azimuth/elevation include the Earth's parallax. The local horizon comes from 720 great-circle rays marched through the LOLA DEM (240 m/px near the pole, 960 m/px to 75°S, up to 600 km) with exact spherical geometry, so lunar curvature is included and no refraction is applied. Power uses the true solar disk fraction above the terrain and a vertical Sun-tracking array. "Earth in view" means Earth's centre clears the terrain (plus an optional margin); a direct-to-Earth link additionally needs a DSN antenna above 10° that is itself in line of sight of the site, with the Moon's elevation at each complex from Astronomy Engine and the antenna's position from the Earth's rotation.

Validation. Against JPL Horizons for observers on the lunar surface (three sites, including Apollo 11 in 1969), Sun and Earth elevations agree within 9″. The 20-year average illumination at Connecting Ridge C1/C2 is 87.7%/78.0%, against the published 88.0%/78.1% (Gläser et al. 2018). Shackleton's permanently shadowed floor correctly stays dark. Our two independent engines (per-pixel GPU ray-marching for the maps, CPU horizon masks for the numbers) agree on lit vs shadowed in 400 of 400 test instants, and their one-year sunlight maps agree within 0.2 percentage points at all ten terrain-modelled sites.

Benefits. When hardware or launch delays force a new date or site, a team can evaluate alternatives in seconds instead of juggling Quickmap, Moon Trek and Horizons tables. The same tool explains to students why a ridge 20 km from Shackleton has 88% sunlight while the crater floor has none.

Tools. HTML, CSS, JavaScript (ES modules, Canvas 2D, WebGL2), Node.js and Python for the data pipeline, Astronomy Engine (MIT). A Node.js unit-test suite (205 checks, including synthetic terrain with analytic answers) runs in GitHub Actions; the app ships with a strict Content-Security-Policy and no third-party requests. No build step and no server: it runs from static hosting such as GitHub Pages. Source code: https://github.com/ValtielCs/penumbra

SI use. Most of the code, the tests, the documentation, the slides and the demo video were written with an AI coding assistant (Claude, Anthropic) under the team's direction; the video and the slides carry a visible "SI-assisted" mark, and every number is reproducible with the scripts in the repository.
